summary: Project M.O.G.O. (Medical Overseer & Guardian Orbital) is a fully autonomous, offline-capable digital flight surgeon designed for deep space exploration. Built to overcome communication delays with Earth, it empowers astronauts to independently manage medical emergencies, psychological health, and microgravity hazards. The system runs entirely on localized edge computing with a lightweight, zero-dependency frontend, requiring no cloud connectivity. By instantly analyzing live biometrics and environmental data, M.O.G.O. anticipates health crises and guides crews through specialized zero-gravity medical protocols, serving as a critical, standalone lifeline for long-duration missions.
details: Project M.O.G.O. (Medical Overseer & Guardian Orbital) is an autonomous, offline-capable clinical decision support system (CDSS) and digital flight-medicine console built for long-duration deep-space missions where communication delays with Earth make real-time ground medical support impossible. What It Does & How It Works Operating on an evidence-based observation framework—nothing is diagnosed; everything is evidenced—M.O.G.O. continuously monitors six core crew physiological signals: Heart Rate Variability (HRV rMSSD in ms), Heart Rate (bpm), Arterial Oxygen Saturation (\text{SpO}_2 in %), Sleep Architecture (hours), Core Temperature (°C), and Exercise Output (minutes). Real-Time Telemetry Stream: Simulated crew telemetry (demo_fixtures/vitals.json) streams over a local FastAPI WebSocket (/ws/vitals) with interactive playback speed controls (0.5\times to 10\times) and live anomaly injection. Deterministic Anomaly Detection (src/compute/detect.py): Rather than relying on opaque black-box models, M.O.G.O. computes personal rolling 30-day baselines (z-scores) for each astronaut and applies a 48-hour multi-signal co-deviation rule to flag coupled physiological stressors across metrics. NASA Open Science Literature Layer & Guardrail (src/agent/explanation.py): Every triggered alert pairs exact mathematical deviation metrics with peer-reviewed studies from the NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSD-379, OSD-194, OSD-665), NASA GeneLab (GLDS-114), and the NASA Technical Reports Server (NASA NTRS-20150016964). A deterministic post-check guardrail enforces strict compliance with NASA flight medicine standards by blocking unauthorized clinical diagnoses or prescribing language. Live Console Visualization: The interface renders real-time physiological charts overlaid with personal baseline shaded tolerance bands, giving crew members immediate situational awareness. Key Benefits 100% Offline Edge Autonomy: Runs locally with zero cloud connectivity required, eliminating vulnerability to deep-space communication blackouts or latency. Personalized Physiological Tracking: Adapts to each astronaut's evolving microgravity baseline over a rolling 30-day window rather than relying on static, one-size-fits-all terrestrial thresholds. Reduced Cognitive Overload: Filters raw telemetry streams into correlated, multi-signal alerts backed by direct scientific citations, helping crews and flight surgeons focus on actionable physiological trends. Verifiable & Auditable Outputs: Every alert exposes the exact z-score math, co-deviation window, and source NASA study URL. Intended Impact Designed for missions aboard the International Space Station, Lunar Gateway, and future Mars transits, Project M.O.G.O. empowers crews to independently detect early signs of autonomic modulation, cardiovascular deconditioning, circadian disruption, and microgravity stressors before they escalate into medical emergencies. Beyond spaceflight, its lightweight, offline-first architecture provides a blueprint for autonomous health monitoring in remote terrestrial environments such as polar research stations, submarines, and off-grid field medicine. Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software Used Languages & Backend: Python 3.10+, FastAPI, Uvicorn, and WebSockets for low-latency local telemetry streaming and deterministic compute pipelines. Frontend: A lightweight, zero-dependency browser console (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) engineered for minimal compute overhead. Hardware Target: Designed to run on localized spacecraft edge-computing nodes without external server infrastructure. Testing & Validation: pytest suite (tests/) validating personal z-score calculations, planted multi-signal anomaly triggers, clean baseline bounds, and anti-diagnostic post-checks using structured JSON telemetry fixtures. Scientific Data Sources: Peer-reviewed study metadata and findings curated from NASA OSDR, NASA GeneLab, and NASA NTRS. What Makes the Project Creative Most AI health concepts either overwhelm users with raw data or introduce safety risks through hallucinated black-box diagnoses. M.O.G.O. takes a deliberately disciplined hybrid approach: pairing deterministic, transparent z-score and 48-hour cross-signal mathematics with an automated NASA Open Science citation engine and an active anti-diagnostic guardrail. By turning peer-reviewed spaceflight literature into real-time, edge-computed telemetry context inside a zero-dependency console, M.O.G.O. bridges rigorous flight medicine with autonomous spacecraft computing. Factors Our Team Considered Deep-Space Communication Latency: Ensuring every component—from WebSocket streaming to UI rendering—operates locally with zero external dependencies. Clinical Safety & Regulatory Guardrails: Adhering strictly to NASA flight medicine principles by prohibiting automated medical diagnoses and verifying compliance via automated post-checks. Individual Baseline Drift in Microgravity: Accounting for physiological adaptation in space by evaluating deviations against personal 30-day rolling statistics and multi-signal correlations rather than isolated single-point spikes. System Reliability & Reproducibility: Building interactive replay speed controls, deterministic math rules, and comprehensive unit tests on clearly labeled simulated telemetry so flight surgeons and evaluators can safely stress-test edge cases.
